title: How fast
hook: in the commentaries, many mind-moments pass while one moment of matter lasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body's matter: five sense doors, the life faculty, and the heat and food that keep a living body being made. Your line: living matter.

There's a short passage in the Buddha's discourses that sounds almost like a shrug. He says he can't think of anything that changes as quickly as the mind. So quickly, he adds, that it isn't easy to find a comparison for it. No number, no measurement, just a teacher admitting that the mind outruns his similes. The Abhidhamma and its commentaries didn't leave it there. They tried to measure it anyway.
screen: `NOTHING CHANGES SO QUICKLY.` → `HARD TO FIND A SIMILE.` → `THEY TRIED TO MEASURE IT.`

segments.voice: Start with the smallest unit. A moment of mind, a khana, has three phases: it arises, it stands, it dissolves. Then the next one arises. In this picture, nothing in between holds still long enough to be a self watching from the side. Each moment does its one job and is gone. Now set matter beside it. Matter also arises and passes, but more slowly: one moment of matter, the manual says, lasts as long as seventeen moments of mind. So while one moment of matter in your hand comes and goes, a whole run of mental moments has arisen, seen, felt and vanished. Now a blink. In the time it takes the eyelids to close and open, tradition says, a great many mind-moments pass. Some later teachers reach for huge numbers, and those can be held loosely. The point isn't the arithmetic. It's the direction: whatever you call this second is already a crowd of moments, each gone before you could name it. Why measure at all? Because of the Buddha's shrug. If nothing changes as quickly as the mind, nothing you're feeling right now is going to stay. A sharp word, a craving, a wave of fear: by the time you notice it, it's already becoming something else. The speed isn't meant to make you dizzy. It's meant to loosen the grip.
screen: `ARISE, STAND, DISSOLVE.` · `MATTER LASTS SEVENTEEN MIND-MOMENTS.` · `A BLINK IS A CROWD OF MOMENTS.` · then, large: `THE SPEED LOOSENS THE GRIP.`

segments.voice: Rest your open eyes on something nearby, then blink once, slowly, and notice the light going, the dark, and the light returning, and how the thing you were looking at seems to be waiting there, unchanged. Then let the breath carry you, and each time you remember, blink once more and watch the whole small drama happen.
How fast. In the manual, one moment of matter lasts while seventeen moments of mind arise and pass, and a blink holds a great many. Today's word.
Your line: faster than a blink. Whatever you're feeling now is already on its way to something else. That's day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the three phases of a mind-moment and the manual's comparison of mind-moments to moments of matter, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to notice how quickly experience changes.

chat.says: Why would Buddhist teachers bother measuring how fast the mind changes?
options: To loosen the grip: if nothing changes faster than the mind, no feeling of yours will stay.
To get exact numbers, so a student can count each mind-moment while sitting.
To show that the mind holds still while the body keeps changing around it.
chat.meaning: The Buddha said nothing changes as quickly as the mind. The measuring points one way: what you feel now won't stay, and that loosens the grip.

khana.meaning: a moment of mind, which arises, stands and dissolves

mind-moments.meaning: the tiny units the mind runs on, each gone in a flash

Abhidhamma.meaning: the higher teaching, the third basket of the Pali canon

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1.48, nothing changes as quickly as the mind

Abhidhammattha Sangaha VI (Compendium of Matter), the arising and passing of matter

notes: AN 1.48 paraphrased (numbering varies by edition; some count it AN 1.48, others AN I.10). Confirm reference and wording.
Three phases (uppada, thiti, bhanga) and 'one moment of matter lasts seventeen mind-moments' stated from Abhidhammattha Sangaha IV/VI; confirm.

'In a blink a great many mind-moments pass': the commentaries give very large figures (e.g. for a lightning flash or the snap of a finger); the script gives no figure and invites the listener to hold such numbers loosely. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with that framing.
The Sautrantika and other schools held different views on momentariness; not raised here (day 1091 covers another school).
